title: A. INTRODUCTION
summary: Inspector General report on the CIA's failed attempt to overthrow Fidel Castro's Cuban regime via covert paramilitary operation. Evaluates organization, staffing, planning, paramilitary conduct, intelligence support, training, and security; excludes detailed military-phase analysis and judgments on non-Agency officials. Annexes trace policy evolution: Eisenhower's March 1960 policy paper, February 1961 Kennedy briefing paper, and March-April 1961 pre-invasion planning papers. Based on about 125 employee interviews and document review.

title: B. HISTORY OF THE PROJECT
summary: Covers the history of the Cuban covert project from 1959 to the April 17, 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion and its defeat. Eisenhower approved the CIA paper 'A Program of Covert Action Against the Castro Regime' on March 17, 1960, authorizing four components: a Cuban exile organization, a propaganda offensive, an internal clandestine intelligence apparatus, and an exile paramilitary force. Budget was $4.4 million.

summary: Describes a 1959-1960 CIA covert program against Cuba: a policy paper backing a clandestine resistance program via a Cuban exile council front with private-businessman cover; preparatory steps including a paramilitary staff, a three-volume operational study of Latin American targets, a plan to train Cuban exile paramilitary instructors in a third country for infiltration, creation of WH/4 branch (January 1960, 40 staff), a Panama training site search, and a Miami reconnaissance for facilities.

title: 8. On 18 January 1960 the WH Division organized Branch
key_items: Talila
summary: The text describes the CIA's early 1960 planning to oust Castro: a three-volume operational study and a December 1959 plan to train Cuban exile paramilitary instructors; the founding of Branch WH/4 in January 1960 with about 40 staff; a Panama training site search; Miami reconnaissance; and efforts to form a unified anti-Castro political front and radio station. In March 1960 the President was briefed on progress, paramilitary timelines, and funding ($900,000, later about $1.9 million). Special Group discussions followed, and the branch grew to 588 staff by April 1961.

title: 16. The activities described to the President

nodes.title: 16. The activities described to the President (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the Agency's Castro project becoming a major activity with top policy sanction, consuming full-time personnel of a rapidly expanding branch, needing detailed oversight and liaison with other agencies. Covers the 24 March 1960 approval by the DCI with an initial $900,000 for FY1960, 85% obligated by 7 April, and an additional $1,000,000 obligated by 30 June. Notes the DCI's pledge to recruit people worldwide and the branch growing from 40 to 588 personnel by April 1961, excluding air operations staff.

nodes.title: PER
PER (intro)
Propaganda Activity
nodes.summary: Describes early Project efforts (1960): organizing an exile front group, propaganda and paramilitary programs, and acquiring Florida sites for training and office space. Covers the 'Bender Group' cover businessmen organization and the FRD formed 11 May 1960. Details propaganda work: Miami radio broadcasts into Cuba, Avance exile publication, Latin American operations, marine broadcast boat, and Swan Island radio station. Notes paramilitary training in Panama and Useppa Island screening, Miami base opening, communications site, safe houses, and liaison with INS, USIA, FCC, Defense and State departments.

nodes.title: Uneasy Front
nodes.summary: Describes the uneasy Cuban exile 'front' (FRD) with Agency case officers: power struggles, Cuban leaders pushing for a large-scale invasion, press leaks in Mexico (Radio Swan), a defector's remark that too many Americans were handing out money, and a June 1960 NSC briefing on a 500-man paramilitary training goal (about 25 teams, an exile air force, maritime support). Also covers doubts about a purely clandestine effort, air and small-unit training starting in Panama, and FRD resistance to moving to Mexico over budget ($500,000 requested versus $131,000 offered).

nodes.title: Training Panama
nodes.summary: Describes CIA-era planning for a Cuban exile paramilitary operation: building an exile air force and maritime support, doubts about purely clandestine efforts, training in Panama (pilots, infiltration teams), FRD resistance to relocating to Mexico, and a 500-trainee paramilitary plan. Covers the three-phase operational plan (guerrilla groups in Pinar del Rio, Escambray, Sierra Maestra; Isle of Pines assault; Havana airassault), escalating budgets (~$25M, extra $10M), and anti-Castro propaganda via Radio Swan, a newspaper, and comic books.

Early 1960 CIA Cuban exile project: Bender Group cover, FRD formed 11 May 1960, Radio Swan and Miami broadcasts, Avance publication, marine broadcast boat, Panama paramilitary training, Useppa Island screening, Miami base, INS/USIA/FCC/State/Defense liaison. Covers FRD power struggles, a June 1960 NSC plan for 500 trainees (about 25 teams, exile air force, maritime support), Mexico relocation budget dispute ($500,000 requested vs. $131,000 offered), and a three-phase operational plan with budgets of about $25M plus $10M, plus propaganda via radio, newspaper, and comics.

nodes.title: POPSET
Maritime Operations
nodes.summary: Covers the 1960 Cuba project (POPSET): a failed 1960s airdrop and a captured, executed paramilitary agent; several successful maritime operations hampered by weather and a single available boat; Castro's arms buildup and tightened internal security; the strike force concept rising in September 1960 under a Marine colonel; Nicaragua offering Puerto Cabezas airstrip; delayed Special Forces trainers; November 1960 shift to conventional military training in Guatemala and Miami recruiting; strike force strength growth to 1,390 by April 1961; and budget shortfalls resolved by a $28.2M supplement.

nodes.title: Freedom Fund Campaign
nodes.summary: Describes the Cuban Freedom Fund Campaign (Nov 1960) soliciting donations for Radio Swan (budgeted $900,000 for FY1961, received only $330) and Bohemia magazine (126,000 circulation). Covers FRD faction infighting, failed unity, delays in provisional government planning and the ultimatum over the Revolutionary Council chair, and the FRD's effective counterintelligence and security service (86 employees, 37 trained officers). Also covers early-1961 training problems, Nicaragua airstrip and new training sites, tank operator training at Fort Knox, and policy stalls during the U.S. administration transition, including the 19 January 1961 Special Group meeting.

nodes.title: Preparations Endorsed
nodes.summary: Describes the Bay of Pigs preparations: a January 22 meeting endorsed the project; on January 28 the new President authorized continued activities and the tactical paramilitary plan went to the Joint Chiefs, who gave a favorable evaluation by February 6. On February 17 the Agency presented a paper with three courses of action against Castro, arguing guerrilla groups were infeasible and advocating a surprise landing by a brigade. The project was told a decision was at least two weeks away, so force expansion was withheld. Underground operations continued with boat and airdrop missions and growing agent infiltration, and Miami Base staffing reached 160 by invasion day. Strike timing and policy authorizations stayed unsettled until the last moment.

Covers the 1960-61 POPSET Cuba project: failed airdrops and maritime operations hampered by weather and limited boats; Castro's buildup; the strike force under a Marine colonel, growing to 1,390 by April 1961, with budget supplement. Also the Freedom Fund Campaign for Radio Swan and Bohemia, FRD infighting, counterintelligence, training problems, and policy stalls during the transition. Finally, Bay of Pigs preparations: endorsement by the new President, Joint Chiefs' favorable evaluation, the February 17 paper proposing a surprise brigade landing, deferred force expansion, continued underground operations, and unsettled strike timing until the last moment.

Early 1960 CIA project training Cuban exiles against Castro: Bender Group cover, FRD formed May 1960, Radio Swan and Miami broadcasts, Panama training, Useppa screening, liaison agencies, FRD power struggles, a June 1960 NSC plan for 500 trainees, a Mexico relocation budget dispute, and a three-phase plan of about $35M. POPSET (1960-61) covers failed airdrops and maritime operations, a strike force growing to 1,390, propaganda campaigns, infighting, and Bay of Pigs preparations including the February 17 brigade-landing paper and unsettled timing.

nodes.title: OP
nodes.summary: Covers the lead-up to the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion: Agency planning delays pending the Mexico City conference, sabotage raids, revised plans presented to the President, FRD leadership changes and Miro Cardona's election as Council chairman, Radio Swan broadcasts, suspension of Cuban overflights, and the March-April preparations. It then details the April 15 air strikes, D-Day landing at the Zapata Peninsula beaches, the cancelled follow-up air strikes, Castro's counterattacks, the brigade's collapse and failed resupply, and its final messages. It closes with an evaluation concluding the failure stemmed mainly from the Agency's inadequate organization, staffing, and direction of the project rather than the President's cancellation of the D-Day air strikes.

summary: CIA's Castro project, a top-sanctioned activity with full-time staff growing from 40 to 588 by April 1961, approved March 1960 with $900,000 initial funding and $1,000,000 more. Covers the 1960-61 training of Cuban exiles (Bender Group, FRD, Radio Swan, Panama, POPSET), funding plans, and the Bay of Pigs invasion: planning delays, sabotage, air strikes, landing, collapse, and evaluation blaming Agency organization and direction rather than the President's cancelled air strikes.

nodes.title: D. EVALUATION OF ORGANIZATION AND COMMAND STRUCTURE
D. EVALUATION OF ORGANIZATION AND COMMAND STRUCTURE (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the organization and command structure of a covert project in the Western Hemisphere Division, an operating branch under the DD/P. The chief lacked task-force-level independence and needed DD/P decisions on policy and operations, with the DD/P delegating much to his Deputy for Covert Action; offices were in separate buildings. WH Division chief partially in chain of command, signing cables until the invasion and supervising staffing, with diminished role over time. DD/P reported to the DCI and DDCI, who represented the Agency at 5412 Special Group meetings. The DCI delegated major decisions, relying on the DDCI for air operations and on project military officers, which deprived him of objective counsel.

nodes.title: Fragmentation of Authority
nodes.summary: Describes mismanagement in an Agency project: authority was fragmented among the project chief, Paramilitary Staff military chief, and busy senior officials, with too many echelons and briefers not doing day-to-day work. Also notes the COPS was warned but did not get involved, the three Senior Staffs were not fully consulted and were ignored, due to WH/4 chiefs' inadequate skill and inexperience, and the Project Review Committee never reviewed the project.

nodes.title: Independence of DPD
nodes.summary: Describes the Agency's Development Projects Division (DPD), which insisted on remaining independent outside the project's organizational structure despite its central role in airdrops, Cuban pilot training, airbase operations, volunteer transport, and aircraft procurement. The project chief had no command authority over air operations, and the split left the two units without daily staff coordination, with separate headquarters and field representatives causing confusion. An October 1960 recommendation to integrate DPD under WH/4 was rejected, and the failure was blamed on personality friction and service rivalry. A large Miami forward base with vague duties duplicated operations, leaving the Agency unable to marshal its forces effectively.

Describes the command and organization of a covert Western Hemisphere Division project under the DD/P: the chief lacked independence, DD/P and DCI delegated decisions, and authority was fragmented among the project chief, Paramilitary Staff, and senior officials, with ignored warnings, unconsulted Senior Staffs, and no Project Review Committee review. The Development Projects Division stayed independent despite central roles in airdrops, pilot training, and aircraft procurement, with no command authority over air operations. An October 1960 integration proposal was rejected, and a redundant Miami forward base left forces poorly coordinated.

summary: Evaluates CIA's Bay of Pigs failure: cancelled air strikes were not the sole cause, as the project may have been doomed given Castro's strength and Soviet materiel. Fundamental cause was the Agency's failure to organize, staff, and control the project with top personnel, plus serious operational mistakes, unaddressed dangers, grave judgment errors, and lack of unbiased high-level scrutiny. Describes the WH Division project's command structure: chief lacked independence, authority was fragmented, warnings ignored, reviews bypassed. Development Projects Division stayed independent without air command; October 1960 integration proposal rejected; redundant Miami base poorly coordinated.

title: E. EVALUATION OF STAFFING

nodes.title: E. EVALUATION OF STAFFING (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the staffing evaluation of an intelligence project (WH/4). In April 1960 the DCI pledged to recall key personnel, but staffing was done by routine negotiation with employees' current offices, not directed assignment. Key spots were filled early without anticipating growth, so supervisors ended up overseeing 15-20 times more people, and no senior officers worked full time. April 1962 Relative Retention Lists show many WH/4 officers (GS-12 to GS-15) were rated in the lowest tier, about 21% in the lowest tenth.

nodes.title: PR
nodes.summary: Garbled excerpt from a historical intelligence-agency report on staffing a project. Covers: personnel assigned were often not the best and some were disposal cases; long unfilled slots (counterintelligence, case officer assistant, Guatemala CI, radio announcer, base chiefs) needed outside recruitment; a personnel shortage forced crash-basis work and long hours; few staff spoke Spanish, so senior officers were pulled in as interpreters; skilled staff were misused as handholders or stevedores; and staffing was defective due to division and branch power over assets. Many excellent staff still performed well and developed.

nodes.title: BOP
nodes.summary: Describes the Bay of Pigs (Cuban operation) CIA-style evaluation. Covers praise for staff effort and support quality, criticism of poor organization and management, obstacles including the 'non-attributability' myth, negotiations with Armed Services over equipment and training, and an overly large military enterprise. Then evaluates planning: the 1960 Eisenhower-approved guerrilla build-up plan versus the 1961 amphibious assault of 1,500 soldiers, which were largely untrained for guerrilla warfare.

summary: Evaluation of staffing for intelligence project WH/4: in April 1960 the DCI pledged to recall key personnel, but staff were obtained by negotiation with current offices. Key posts were filled early without planning for growth, leaving supervisors overseeing 15-20 times more people and no senior officers full time. April 1962 Relative Retention Lists rated many WH/4 officers (GS-12 to GS-15) in the lowest tier, about 21% in the lowest tenth. Staff quality was uneven, with long-vacant slots, shortages forcing crash work, few Spanish speakers, skilled staff misused, and divided control over assets. Bay of Pigs evaluation praises staff effort, criticizes management, notes the 'non-attributability' myth and military negotiations, and contrasts the 1960 guerrilla plan with the 1961 assault of largely untrained troops.

nodes.summary: Excerpt from a declassified CIA history of the 1961 Bay of Pigs (Cuba) operation. Covers: the original covert plan being obsolete by November 1960 due to Castro's Soviet-backed strength; a revised plan with air infiltration, a 650-700 man amphibious landing, and air strikes; Eisenhower's directive to proceed; policy disputes over US pilots, airbases, air-strike timing, and Puerto Cabezas; conflicting views between political acceptability and military effectiveness; Kennedy's January 1961 briefings and approval to continue without authorizing invasion; and successive concept papers leading to the April 1961 plan made politically acceptable as a guerrilla uprising.

nodes.title: SPOSG
SPOSG (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers the 1961 Cuban invasion planning: four site characteristics (night landing, air operations from seized base, build-up period, guerrilla terrain), the shift from Trinidad to Zapata for airfield needs, a diversionary Oriente landing, and dawn air strikes. It argues the invasion was no longer a coordinated guerrilla-assist effort: estimates of 1,200 guerrillas and 7,000 'insurgents' were vague and unverified, with no confirmed control or radio links. Supply airdrops failed and Castro's security forces arrested agents and neutralized guerrilla groups.

nodes.summary: Describes the 1961 Bay of Pigs-style invasion plan: the Agency hoped the brigade's landing would spark defections and an uprising, acting as a catalyst without any organized resistance in place. It contrasts the 1,500-man brigade with Castro's forces (32,000 Revolutionary Army, 200,000 militia, large Bloc arms). It questions the justification for proceeding, especially the Zapata area's poor guerrilla terrain and the lack of contingency or rescue planning. It notes the untested argument that cancelled D-Day airstrikes were essential.

nodes.summary: Describes the Agency's matching of a 1,500-man brigade against Castro's forces after an amphibious landing, citing USIB estimates (Nov 1960, Feb 1961): Revolutionary Army 32,000, militia 200,000, and over 30,000 tons of Bloc arms worth $30 million. Criticizes the invasion decision as unjustified in later stages, notes the Zapata area offered poor guerrilla terrain and no breakout or rescue planning, and disputes the theory that an uprising would follow a successful landing, since cancelled D-Day airstrikes were never tested.

nodes.summary: Describes the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion critique: the Agency pitted a 1,500-man brigade against Castro's forces (Revolutionary Army 32,000; militia 200,000; heavy Bloc arms). It questions the invasion's justification, the Zapata landing area's poor guerrilla terrain, and lack of survival/rescue planning. It notes reliance on uprising theory, the Joint Chiefs' approval based on oral briefings and assumptions of air support, and four planning mistakes: no objective appraisal, failure to advise cancellation to the President, failure to recognize the operation had outgrown the Agency, and lack of formal written approvals. Warnings were ignored amid pressure and policy restrictions; cancellation would have been embarrassing but would have averted failure.

nodes.title: which
nodes.summary: Describes the Bay of Pigs failure: the invasion brigade was not isolated or supported, and the Agency had no evidence of an internal uprising or mass Cuban resistance joining the invaders. A successful lodgment would have been dubious without overt U.S. armed support. The Agency gambled on the operation at rapidly decreasing odds, choosing between retreat and a dubious victory, which caused death, property loss, and damage to U.S. prestige.

Analysis of the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion: a 1,500-man brigade faced Castro's 32,000 Revolutionary Army, 200,000 militia, and over $30 million in Bloc arms. The critique covers the Zapata area's poor guerrilla terrain, lack of rescue or contingency planning, and an untested uprising theory tied to cancelled D-Day airstrikes. It also cites four planning mistakes, including unapproved oral Joint Chiefs briefings, and concludes the brigade lacked internal support or U.S. backing, so retreat was the only realistic option.

nodes.title: 42. The project had lost its covert nature by November
nodes.summary: Describes how the CIA-backed Cuban invasion project lost its covert nature by November 1960. Press reported on Cuban recruiting and training for over three months before the invasion, so plausible denial was illusory. Insisting on non-attributability caused absurdities and delays: obsolete B-26s were used instead of requested A-5s, a surgical tent and a modern rifle (even though surplus) were withheld, and everything was traced to the U.S.

nodes.title: 4k. U.S. policy called for a covert operation and assigned
nodes.summary: Describes the Bay of Pigs-era policy failures: a covert operation was assigned to the CIA, and after it became public the Agency failed to inform higher authority that it had exceeded its charter. Had an overt joint national task force continued, greater manpower and effective support would have been available, avoiding costly delays in obtaining armed services support. Policy was formed piecemeal, with successive restrictions narrowing the margin of error; a late presidential restriction came as the brigade neared the Cuban shore, and earlier action might have averted the invasion and lost prestige.

nodes.summary: Excerpts from a declassified CIA-style review of the 1961 Bay of Pigs (Cuba) operation. Covers: the April 16 last-minute cancellation of D-Day air strikes by the President via the Secretary of State and Deputy Directors, made without direct contact with military chiefs, and the failure to circulate formal planning papers with requests for confirmation; the lack of air-command principle understanding among advisors. Also covers the project's shifting scope and staffing growth (235 to 588 personnel), brigade size changes (200-300 to 1,390 actual), logistics delays, budget growth ($4.4M estimate to over $46M), and missing bases and facilities that hampered the project.

Covers the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion planning and failures: site choice shift from Trinidad to Zapata, flawed guerrilla-support assumptions, failed airdrops and arrests, a 1,500-man brigade versus Castro's large forces, untested uprising theory, cancelled D-Day air strikes, loss of covert cover by press, policy restrictions, bureaucratic and logistical problems, budget and staffing growth, and conclusion that retreat was the only realistic option.

title: G. THE MIAMI OPERATING BASE ~

nodes.title: G. THE MIAMI OPERATING BASE ~ (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the Miami Operating Base (WH/4), activated late April 1960 as a forward base for Cuban refugee and exile liaison and U.S. law enforcement coordination, with little operational activity until September 1960. Covers confused relationships with WH/4 headquarters; DD/P Chief of Operations accepting need for operational personnel but opposing a second headquarters; Assistant for Covert Action stressing coordination-only role; DD/P's August and November concerns about duplicating Headquarters functions; and noting that duplication of effort already existed by then.

nodes.title: Head-
Head- (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Headquarters and Miami Base overlapping, competing operations handling the same agents (Miami excluded air ops but aided drops). Headquarters saw Miami as support only; Miami saw itself as a station, but a several-hundred-person station would be hard to conceal and costly. Agency leaders' limits hurt: Guatemala-trained resistance organizers lacked maritime infiltration capability in September, losing months. The 6 Oct 1960 letter vaguely gave the base chief authority over project personnel and funds. By the invasion, Miami had 31 FI agents in Cuba, all recruited by the base.

nodes.title: The CI Section
nodes.summary: Describes the counterintelligence (CI) section, begun mid-July 1960, with 39 selected educated Cubans trained as future Cuban intelligence officers plus a reserve of 100 older non-political civil servants. The paramilitary (PM) section opened late 1960 with one officer recruiting Cuban leaders for Guatemala camps; a second PM officer arrived in August and infiltration by boat began. By 15 November, 39 staff were at Miami base plus 44 Communications staff. By 15 April 1961, 160 persons were assigned across FI, CI, political action, propaganda, support, PM, security, communications. Havana Station closed; Headquarters took control of stay-behind assets while Miami focused on agent training and infiltration.

nodes.title: PM Support Role
nodes.summary: PM support role under tight Headquarters control, causing confusion and uncontrolled channels; Key West PM officers sometimes contacted Headquarters directly, bypassing the Miami base chief. Headquarters decisions were sometimes conveyed inconsistently to Miami, and the base chief was often uninformed. Miami case officers kept agents reporting by secret writing but resented Headquarters taking over agents who reported by radio. Headquarters case officers suspected Miami officers of trying to steal agents; one agent received unauthorized promises from Headquarters, leading to months of unmanageability and perceived Headquarters meddling.

nodes.title: Examples of Confusion
nodes.summary: Describes confusion in Miami case officer operations: Headquarters both competed with and reviewed Miami's actions, undermining objectivity. Cites a costly lubricating-oil sabotage fiasco, a cable asking whether Headquarters would arrange an operation, and frequent temporary-duty trips between Washington and Miami. Base chief requested clearer requirements and authority (Dec 1960, Mar 1961). May 1961 memo urged single control, noting divided control caused duplicative, counterproductive efforts and wasted time, money, personnel, and agent assets.

Describes the Head- section on overlapping Headquarters and Miami Base operations running competing efforts with the same agents, with Miami seen as support only and leadership limits delaying maritime infiltration. Covers the CI and PM sections' 1960-61 buildup to 160 staff, Havana Station's closure, and PM support under tight Headquarters control causing bypassed channels, inconsistent decisions, agent poaching disputes, and confusion. Ends with a May 1961 memo urging single control to end wasteful duplication.

nodes.title: Detain
Detain (intro)
H. INTELLIGENCE SUPPORT
nodes.summary: Describes the WH/4 Branch's dual role as a Cuba task force and Headquarters desk for Cuba, supporting Havana Station and Santiago Base until diplomatic relations broke. Covers its intelligence section: personnel shortages, reporting on political, economic and Communist Party matters, a late-1960 shift to military intelligence without high-level sources, and transmitting reports to other units. Notes Havana Station's stay-behind agent net of about 27 people when the embassy closed on 3 January 1961. Finally, criticizes placing the September 1960 G-2 unit under the paramilitary section, a grave error.

nodes.title: Function of G-2 Unit
nodes.summary: Describes the paramilitary G-2 unit of four officers and secretaries that prepared intelligence annexes for invasion plans, drawing on FI section intelligence, reports, photo and cartographic intelligence, armed services reports, and agent messages from Cuba, with fast informal liaison. It notes the G-2 unit adversely affected the regular FI section, which lost personnel to the PM unit, was excluded from WH/4 staff meetings and the war room, could not review PM operational cables, and lacked photographic intelligence clearance.

nodes.title: Lack of Liaison
nodes.summary: Describes intelligence failures in a covert operation: no liaison between the two sections (separate buildings until 1960) caused duplicated reports. G-2 chief concentrated all intelligence and its interpretation, while officers deeply engaged in invasion preparations judged that a landing would trigger an uprising, a conclusion that drove the decision to invade. Miami Base received almost no intelligence support, lacked an intelligence section or officer with proper clearance, had no photo intelligence, no coverage of Cuban beaches or the political situation, no analysis of Special Intelligence, and no mechanism to flag critical material.

Section 'Detain (intro)' covers the WH/4 Branch's dual role as Cuba task force and Headquarters desk, intelligence support to Havana Station and Santiago Base until diplomatic relations broke, personnel shortages, and reporting shifts (including a late-1960 move to military intelligence); Havana's stay-behind agent net of about 27 when the embassy closed 3 January 1961; criticism of placing the September 1960 G-2 unit under paramilitary, a grave error. The G-2 unit of four prepared invasion annexes, adversely affecting the FI section, which was excluded from meetings and lacked clearances. Lack of liaison caused duplicated reports and misjudgments that an uprising would follow landing; Miami Base received almost no intelligence support.

nodes.title: I. THE POLITICAL FRONT AND THE RELATION OF CUBANS TO THE PROJECT
key_items: (FRD)
nodes.summary: Describes a planned Cuban opposition front (FRD) conceived by the Agency with the State Department: restore the 1940 constitution, return to 1958 Caracas Declaration principles, pro-Western anti-Communist stance, center-right to center-left politics. Its functions were cover for covert action, rallying anti-Castro groups, and a possible provisional government. Batistianos and far-left were excluded, causing problems. Covers figures Carrillo, Rasco, Artime, Varona, the organizing committee formed May 1960, and the political spectrum.

nodes.title: SG

fairly broad range of political views. They were joined June 1960 by Aureliano Sanchez Arango who claimed leadership (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the 1960 formation of the FRD (Frente Revolucionario Democratico) against Castro's dictatorship. Covers the original organizers' broad political range, Aurelio Sanchez Arango joining in June 1960 and claiming leadership of the AAA group, and both Sanchez Arango and Varona claiming labor followings. Notes a manifesto issued in Mexico City on 22 June 1960 pledging a representative democracy under the 1940 constitution, free elections within 18 months, banning the Communist party, and a social and economic program. Varona was chosen as coordinator and general manager, but rivalry with Sanchez Arango caused lasting unity problems.

nodes.title: Change in Policy
nodes.summary: Describes a 1960 CIA-backed shift in policy: the FRD (Revolutionary Democratic Front) was originally the sole channel for project aid, but after Sanchez Arango's threat to assets, the project began supporting other anti-Castro groups, including Bender Group defectors' aid. This diffused effort, hampered FRD unity, sharpened antagonisms, and reduced recruiting. Sardina's MID shifted FRD politics right. The FRD relocated to Mexico City under promised hospitality, but Mexico surveilled and harassed them, so they returned to Miami.

nodes.title: The Bender Group
nodes.summary: Describes the Bender Group, a project political section chief known as 'Frank Bender', whose cover was a plausible-denial U.S. businessmen front to help overthrow Castro. Covers his role arranging meetings with Cubans to merge differences and issue a joint manifesto, Cuban irritation at the guise, his lack of Spanish, the FRD handling passed to a Spanish-fluent officer, and FRD leaders' antagonism after Bender was assigned Cubans outside the FRD framework.

nodes.title: The Rubio Padilla Group
nodes.summary: Covers the Action Movement for Recovery (MAR), led by Juan Rubio Padilla, a conservative group of wealthy landlords backed by Miami businessman William D. Pawley; a 1960 CIA briefing paper touted its claimed widespread resistance network, but MAR was never incorporated into the FRD as Rubio was too conservative. Also covers the Movimiento Revolucionario del Pueblo (MRP) led by Manuel Antonio Ray Rivero, a former Castro minister, who arrived in November 1960, had a strained relationship with the Bender Group, joined the FRD's military aid program in December 1960, and later joined the Revolutionary Council; his unsubstantiated resource claims were accepted uncritically by some project staff.

nodes.title: Contact with Batistianos
nodes.summary: Describes allegations that the project supported former Batista associates. WH/4 had brief contact with ex-Batista leader Sanchez Mosquerra and gave some support, soon called off. Batistianos tried to penetrate the military effort and FRD intelligence screened them out. Some former Constitutional Army members were recruited as soldiers, not politicians. Brigade officers were reportedly clean of Batista ties, but the FRD complained it had no role in selecting them. Jose Miro Cardona, a former Cuban prime minister who broke with Castro, became FRD public relations secretary-general after asylum and safe conduct to the US in October 1960. Miro built FRD unity, helped bring Ray into the Revolutionary Council formed March 20 with Miro as chairman, and visited the Guatemala strike force on March 29 to boost morale. Earlier visits by Artime, Yara, Maceo and Col. Martin Elena were poorly handled, and a U.S. Army officer's ban on Cuban politicians' visits blocked political contact, which the author calls a mistake that left trainees without answers to political questions.

Describes the 1960 formation of the FRD against Castro, its broad political membership, Aureliano Sanchez Arango's leadership claim and the June 22 Mexico City manifesto (representative democracy, elections within 18 months, banning communists). Covers the CIA-backed policy shift, the Bender Group's cover and FRD friction, the MAR and MRP groups, allegations of Batista ties, and Jose Miro Cardona's role in unity and the Revolutionary Council. Notes missed political contacts with trainees.

nodes.title: Visit to Training Camp
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a Bay of Pigs-era history covering: Bender and Miro's efforts to unify the FRD and Miro's role in forming the Revolutionary Council (March 1961); a March 1961 Council visit to the Guatemala training camp to boost troop morale, with prior contact limited and poorly managed; criticism that the CIA's tight control over Cuban contacts hurt morale and loyalty; the operation becoming an American one in exile eyes, weakening cover; CIA progress reports showing it made the plans and decisions; Council members kept isolated in Miami safehouses, uninformed, and used as puppets; and the shift from clandestine to military operation cutting Cuban advisers out.

nodes.summary: Describes Cuban Revolutionary Council members being sidelined during a covert operation (the Bay of Pigs-era project). Cubans were cut out as the project shifted to a military focus, with officers treating Cubans as untrustworthy and the paramilitary and political sections disconnected. Some case officers nonetheless built good rapport with Cubans. Also covers a Cuban government biographic compilation for a future provisional government, and a wealthy Cuban who volunteered for assessment on Useppa Island.

nodes.title: Dealing with Cubans
nodes.summary: Covers problems dealing with Cubans in a Cuba project: military officers gave orders expecting obedience, contract staff (e.g., ship officers) mistreated Cubans causing revolts, mutinies, and departures of capable Cubans. The inspectors found the operation took on a life of its own, and staff lost sight of goals. The text questions whether such operations can succeed with unfavorable attitudes toward other peoples, and warns that condescension toward nationals undermines anti-communist efforts. It also describes the first clandestine air drop over Cuba (28 Sept 1960), which failed when the plane missed the drop zone and the agent was captured, and a Dec 1960 drop where DPD ignored the agent's request, delivering mostly food instead of the requested 1,500 lb of sabotage materiel, causing the agent to refuse further drops.

Covers the 1960 formation of the FRD, its broad membership and Aureliano Sanchez Arango's leadership claim, and the June 1960 Mexico City manifesto. Also covers the CIA-backed policy shift, Bender Group friction, MAR/MRP groups, alleged Batista ties, and Jose Miro Cardona's unity role. Details the March 1961 Revolutionary Council formation and its Guatemala camp visit, CIA control hurting morale, and Council members sidelined as puppets. Notes Cubans cut out as the operation turned military, mistreatment by contract staff causing mutinies, failed 1960 air drops, and a Dec 1960 drop that delivered food instead of requested materiel.

Section 18 says Miami case officers had to interpret separate intelligence reports themselves, without specialist analysis, and were denied other operational intelligence held in the Headquarters paramilitary G-2 unit. Subsections cover the planned Cuban opposition front (FRD), conceived with the State Department to restore the 1940 constitution and oppose Castro. Its exclusion of Batistianos and the far left caused problems. Also covered: the 1960 FRD formation and Mexico City manifesto, the March 1961 Revolutionary Council and CIA control, Cubans sidelined as the operation turned military, failed air drops, and mutinies.

The WH/4 Branch served as both Cuba task force and Headquarters desk, supporting Havana and Santiago until relations broke; it moved to military intelligence in late 1960. Havana kept a stay-behind agent net of about 27 when the embassy closed in January 1961. The September 1960 G-2 unit under paramilitary was a grave error: its four members adversely affected the excluded FI section, and poor liaison caused duplicated reports and misjudgments. Miami Base got almost no intelligence support, and case officers interpreted reports unaided. The planned FRD opposition front, formed with State Department input, excluded Batistianos and the far left, and was later sidelined as the operation turned military, with failed air drops and mutinies.

nodes.title: TED Ra
TED Ra (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a declassified CIA-style report on the 1961 Bay of Pigs air-drop operation. Covers: 30 missions flown to 21 April 1961 with only four recorded successes; the successful drops, concentrated in Pinar del Rio; about 151,000 lbs of arms and equipment airlifted, of which roughly 69,000 lbs were dropped and most captured by Castro forces, leaving agents with about 12,000 lbs; no clandestine personnel drops; no standard air-reception procedure, with confusing coordinates and bizarre light signal patterns; Cuban aircrew and trainer failures and disregarded orders; and divided, poorly coordinated Headquarters command between DPD and WH/4.

nodes.title: Cena Si
nodes.summary: Describes CIA-era operational problems in the Cuba air-drop project: WH/4 and DPD disagreed on doctrine and techniques; every flight plan needed approval from the DDCI and the 5412 Special Group; requests moved slowly from Cuba through Miami and headquarters; scarce radio operators forced slow secret-writing arrangements that caused misunderstanding; and the 30 December drop illustrated confusion over altitude (400, 1,000, or 600 feet).

nodes.title: BOP reel
nodes.summary: Describes failed and mismanaged airdrops to Cuban resistance groups run by DPD and WH/4: poor coordination over drop timing, bundle counts, and cargo weights; a drop repeatedly rescheduled from October to December 30; reliance on dead reckoning, multiple passes and turns that alerted Castro forces, who captured most supplies; blind drops; heavy weapons dropped before groups could use them; unreported drop results; an emergency landing in Jamaica handled poorly; and 1961 studies finding Cuban aircrews inexperienced and undisciplined.

nodes.title: Guatemala DPD Drop Missions: Coordination, Corrective Action, and Pilot Check

nodes.summary: Describes a March mission in which a DPD cable from Guatemala prompted an analysis to refine tactics and coordination with reception teams; at month's end a check pilot flew in a mission crew for the first time, and discrepancies in pilot procedure and crew coordination were noted. It also covers critiques of drop zone compliance, elimination of blind drops, and mission identification. Tardy corrective action is addressed: reliance on an amphibious assault grew, clandestine drop interest waned, and a 28 March decision halted clandestine drops until after the assault, leaving WH/4 officers uninformed and forcing stalled drop requests for 19 to 22 April.

nodes.title: Pret
nodes.summary: A garbled, OCR-scanned Cold War-era CIA report on Cuba operations (1960-61). It covers failed airdrops of arms and supplies to Cuban resistance, with dire messages from resistance groups about unmet promises; the Agency's lack of professional competence, which the Inspector General judged harmful to the resistance. It then details the clandestine maritime program: WH/4's small boat operations, the "Metusa Time," the "Barbara J" mutiny and failed landings, the "Tejana" and "Wasp" yachts, cargo totals, poor planning, a captain commended despite drunkenness, and organizational and Key West base problems.

nodes.title: PPSR OO
key_items: approved by the President in March 1960 included the above
nodes.summary: A CIA-era account of a covert Caribbean/Cuban operation. Covers small-boat operations at Key West (ad hoc, unsupervised, heavy labor), lack of policy on boats, maritime unit coordination failures, purchase and refit costs (~$1.4M on boats, ~$2.68M total maritime), the costly 'Sea Gull' boat case, and a poorly handled naval captain. Also covers training of Cuban underground leaders from 1960 (Useppa Island screening, Panama and Guatemala training sites, Guatemala camp hardships), with trainees poorly used and costs over $1M.

nodes.summary: Describes the 1960–61 CIA-backed paramilitary training of Cuban exile teams (precursor to the Bay of Pigs). Covers training bases in Guatemala, Panama, and New Orleans; trainee numbers and selection; repeated shifting of plans and missions from Headquarters; delayed infiltration (only a few agents landed, none by air or submarine); morale collapse among trainees; poor instruction, lack of equipment and defined training goals; and the absence of a full-time training chief.

nodes.title: Dente
Dente (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes training of Cuban personnel in Miami and Washington on intelligence collection, counterintelligence, psychological warfare, and paramilitary skills, conducted in safe houses by base and case officers. Training was ad hoc, effectiveness unknown; requests to the Office of Training were uncoordinated, and instructors were often misassigned (e.g., stevedoring). A well-planned project would have included a training annex specifying requirements; instead, needs were met piecemeal under difficult conditions with dubious results.

nodes.title: M. SECURITY
nodes.summary: The text describes security weaknesses in the assault on Cuba. The operation was poorly kept secret given its complexity and the many Cuban and American participants. The inspection team did not study security in detail but found weak protection of information from those without a need to know. Cuban participants lacked understanding of the need for secrecy, knew more than necessary, and were not compartmented.

nodes.title: from each other and from Americans to the extent that was neces-
from each other and from Americans to the extent that was neces- (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes security and operational failures in a covert project involving agents sent into Cuba: case officers handling agents redundantly, trained agents sharing identities so one arrest exposes others, poor personal security leading to arrests, and Miami community leaks about boat movements and letters. Also covers lax security by Americans (overheard meeting), inadequate training-camp security and counterintelligence, rushed screening of recruits, weak cover stories and documentation, unsuitable 'tourist' pretenses, failed overflight backstopping, and excessive compartmentation that kept planners from the strike plan.

nodes.title: POPS St
POPS St (intro)
POPS St (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes security lapses in a covert operation: Cuban resistance and the Miami Base were not told of the assault timing, and staff clearances came too late. Guatemala training camps were easily observed and exposed, unlike safer U.S. options. Other Cuban training in Miami, Washington, New Orleans, and Vieques was secret, but only Guatemala became public. Errors, though some security measures were strong, exposed personnel and methods to many uncontrolled people.

nodes.title: N. AMERICANS IN COMBAT
nodes.summary: Covers Americans in the 1961 Cuban invasion: two Agency contract operations officers aboard LCIs fought ashore and later aided rescues; late-1960 doubts about Cuban pilots led to requesting American contract pilots and seamen; three experienced pilots plus Air National Guard-linked recruits were hired under a notional company; Cuban crews were exhausted by day one; Americans volunteered on 18 April, with four American fliers killed or executed; a PBY patrolled for rescue; cover stories and legal/insurance problems for families of the four dead are discussed.

nodes.title: O. CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
nodes.summary: The text is the closing part of an Inspector General survey of the CIA's Cuban operation (Bay of Pigs era). It concludes the Agency drifted from covert resistance-building into an overt military effort, misjudged chances of success, failed to inform policymakers, under-used exiled leaders, lacked assets and information on Castro's regime, had poor organization, unclear command, unused staff, and vague plans. It notes some strengths in logistics, communications, and dedicated personnel. Previous IG reports had flagged similar problems. Ten recommendations follow: use a full-time task force, transfer overt efforts to Defense, add independent intelligence and operational appraisals, clarify policy, and improve air, maritime, language, and assignment practices. It then begins a March 1960 covert action program to replace Castro's regime with a unified Cuban opposition.

Covers security lapses in a covert Cuban operation (Bay of Pigs era): the Miami Base and resistance were not told the assault timing, clearances came late, and Guatemala camps were easily observed and exposed. Describes Americans in the 1961 invasion, including contract officers, pilots and seamen hired under a notional company, volunteers, four American fliers killed or executed, rescue patrols, cover stories, and legal and insurance issues for the families. Closing Inspector General conclusions: the Agency drifted into overt military action, misjudged success, failed to inform policymakers, lacked intelligence, had poor organization, and made ten recommendations.

nodes.title: A PROGRAM OF COVERT ACTION AGAINST THE CASTRO REGIME
1. Objective
nodes.summary: A 1960 CIA document outlining a covert action program to replace the Castro regime in Cuba with a government more acceptable to the U.S. while avoiding the appearance of U.S. intervention. It covers four courses of action: forming a unified Cuban opposition council (the 'Restore the Revolution' slogan, via merger of three groups); a gray propaganda broadcasting facility (likely Swan Island) plus clandestine print distribution; a covert intelligence and action network inside Cuba; and a paramilitary force trained outside Cuba with limited air resupply. It also addresses leadership, calling for a non-ambitious, uncontentious chairman and a later successor selected for U.S. support.

nodes.title: 4. Cover
nodes.summary: Describes CIA support for a Cuban opposition council: CIA actions will be attributed to the council, with CIA personnel documented as its representatives. A screened group of Cubans and U.S. businessmen will act as a second channel for guidance and support. Private funds are sought to strengthen cover, with $100,000 already pledged. A bond issue floated by the council, to be repaid by a future Cuban government, is anticipated at about $2,000,000. Budget: about $3,500,000 required, with $900,000 in CIA funds for FY-1960 and the balance in FY-1961, subject to possible acceleration or policy changes.

A 1960 CIA document outlines a covert program to replace the Castro regime in Cuba with a U.S.-acceptable government while avoiding the appearance of U.S. intervention. It covers a unified Cuban opposition council ('Restore the Revolution'), gray propaganda broadcasting and clandestine print, a covert intelligence network inside Cuba, and a paramilitary force trained abroad. It addresses leadership selection, CIA cover via the council and a screened business channel, private funding ($100,000 pledged), a bond issue (~$2,000,000), a budget of ~$3,500,000, and a recommendation to authorize the program from the Agency's contingency reserve.

Describes POPS St: security lapses in a covert Bay of Pigs-era Cuban operation (Miami Base not told assault timing, late clearances, exposed Guatemala camps); Americans in the 1961 invasion (contract officers, pilots, seamen under notional company, volunteers, four American fliers killed or executed), rescue patrols, cover stories, family legal/insurance issues; Inspector General conclusions (drift into overt military action, misjudged success, uninformed policymakers, poor intelligence and organization, ten recommendations). Also a 1960 CIA covert program to replace Castro with a U.S.-acceptable government: unified opposition council, gray propaganda and clandestine print, internal intelligence network, trained paramilitary force, leadership selection, CIA cover via council and screened business channel, $100,000 private pledge, ~$2,000,000 bond issue, ~$3,500,000 budget, and a recommendation to fund from contingency reserve.

nodes.title: THE POLITICAL OPPOSITION
nodes.summary: Describes the political opposition to the Castro regime. The UIA is in close contact with three opposition groups (Montecristi Autentico Party, National Democratic Front, and others) that back the revolution as originally conceived, many being former 26th of July members and not tied to Batista or Trujillo. They oppose Castro for abandoning the 26th of July platform and for possibly selling out to communist domination. An opposition council or junta is to form within 30 days, using the 20 July 1958 Caracas Manifesto, with suggested points such as calling Castro's regime a new Cuban dictatorship under Sino-Soviet influence.

Covers security and operational failures in a covert Cuba project: redundant case officers, agents sharing identities, poor personal security, Miami leaks, lax American security, weak training-camp counterintelligence, rushed recruit screening, weak covers, failed overflight backstopping, and over-compartmentation. Also covers the Bay of Pigs operation (timing and Guatemala camp exposure, American contractors, pilots and volunteers, four American fliers killed, rescue patrols, family legal issues), Inspector General conclusions and ten recommendations, and a 1960 CIA plan to replace Castro with a U.S.-acceptable government, with funding and structure. Finally, the political opposition: UIA-linked groups, ex-26th of July members opposing Castro's betrayal, and a planned opposition council using the Caracas Manifesto.

nodes.summary: Describes the political opposition to Castro's regime in Cuba: UIA is in close contact with three opposition groups (Montecristi Autentico Party, National Democratic Front, and others) that favor the revolution as originally conceived (many are former 26th of July members) and are not tied to Batista or Trujillo. They oppose Castro for abandoning the 26th of July platform and for apparently selling out to Communist domination. An opposition council or junta is to be formed within 30 days, possibly augmented by other groups, using the slogan "Restore the Revolution." The Caracas Manifesto of 20 July 1958 is noted as containing exploitable points, and the text suggests Castro's regime is a new dictatorship under Sino-Soviet influence.

nodes.title: PROPAGANDA
nodes.summary: Describes a SECRET-marked propaganda plan (Tab C) for Cuba: supporting private opposition broadcasts and establishing a 'gray' radio station, likely on Swan Island, with possible supplementary stations near Havana, scripts prepared in the US. It covers newspaper support (Avance, Diario de la Marina, exile editions printed in the US and smuggled into Cuba), a CIA-controlled inside-Cuba group producing anti-Castro publications, and lecture tours by Cuban exiles in Latin America backed by controlled Western Hemisphere media and American journalists.

nodes.title: FINANCIAL ANNEX
nodes.summary: A financial annex dated 17 February 1961 (Cuba) lists budget figures for FY-1960 and FY-1961 across four categories: Political Action (support of opposition elements and group activities: 150,000 and 800,000), Propaganda (radio operations and programming including transmitter establishment: 400,000 and 700,000; press and publications: 100,000 and 500,000), Paramilitary (infiltration/exfiltration, maritime and air support, material and training: 200,000 and 1,300,000), and Intelligence Collection (50,000 and unspecified). Totals are 900,000 and 3,500,000. A footnote says FY-1961 figures assume major action will not occur until then; accelerating the program would require additional funds.

nodes.title: BACKGROUND:
nodes.summary: A 1960s-era US Agency plan to overthrow the Castro regime: building a broad opposition, clandestine agent networks in Cuba, and paramilitary ground and air forces, with a planned left-of-center Government-in-Exile. It assesses the regime as consolidating control over institutions (media, unions, enterprises, peasantry, internal security, military) despite declining popular support, with the Communist Bloc shielding it from economic troubles. Conclusion: the regime is unlikely to fall on its own, and the US must decide on future support for the opposition.

Describes a CIA-style plan to overthrow Castro's Cuban regime. Covers: UIA contact with three opposition groups (former 26th of July members, not tied to Batista or Trujillo) who oppose Castro's Communist turn; a junta to be formed within 30 days under the slogan "Restore the Revolution"; a secret propaganda plan with radio stations, newspapers, and exile lecture tours; a FY-1960/1961 financial annex (total 900,000 and 3,500,000) for political action, propaganda, paramilitary, and intelligence; and a background assessment that the regime is consolidating control and is unlikely to fall on its own, so the US must decide on future support.

nodes.title: b. Cuba is in economic difficulties but the Commnist
b. Cuba is in economic difficulties but the Commnist (intro)
nodes.summary: The text argues the Castro regime will not fall on its own: it is consolidating control over radio, TV, press, unions, professional groups, nationalized industry, and peasantry, and has eliminated all parties except the Communist Party. Cuba's economic troubles will cause dislocation but not regime collapse, and the Communist bloc will prevent decisive threats. Cuba's regular military is weak now, but within about six months new jets and trained pilots will make a military overthrow infeasible. Cuba poses no direct military threat to the US, but may support subversion, arms, and instability across Latin America, serving Soviet influence.

nodes.title: 4. POSSIBLE COURSES OF ACTION:
nodes.summary: A 1961-style policy memo weighs options against Castro's Cuba: overt US military invasion is excluded; remaining options are (a) intensified economic/political pressure with covert sabotage, (b) a paramilitary landing not appearing as invasion, or (c) gradual infiltration. Economic pressure is judged ineffective (blockade infeasible, arms interdiction easily evaded, sanctions offset by Bloc trade). Infiltration is militarily infeasible; a single landing is cheapest. Joint Chiefs rate the landing a fair chance, with guerrilla fallback; militia reliability is doubtful; US backing is deniable; political costs are low if quick. Dissolving the force would hurt US prestige and anger exile leaders.

nodes.title: 9. CONCLUSIONS:
nodes.summary: Argues that Castro's position is strengthening and an all-out embargo or drastic action may be needed to remove him, warning that failing to do so would let Sino-Soviet influence grow in the Western Hemisphere and weaken U.S. prestige. Suggests a Cuban paramilitary force could overthrow Castro or cause damaging civil war without overt U.S. military action, with embarrassment less costly than a later drastic response. Notes Soviet reaction to Castro's removal would likely be less harmful to U.S. long-range interests than his continuation.

Argues the Castro regime will not fall on its own: it is consolidating control over media, unions, industry, and peasantry, with the Communist Party the only remaining party. Economic troubles will cause dislocation but not collapse, and Bloc support will block decisive threats. Cuba poses no direct military threat to the US but may back subversion in Latin America serving Soviet influence. A 1961-style memo weighs options: overt invasion excluded; economic pressure judged ineffective; infiltration infeasible; a deniable paramilitary landing is cheapest, with guerrilla fallback, doubtful militia reliability, and prestige costs if dropped. Conclusions urge strong action to prevent Sino-Soviet gains, expecting Castro's removal to serve US interests.

Describes a CIA-style plan to overthrow Castro's Cuban regime: contact with three opposition groups (former 26th of July members) opposing Communist turn, a junta within 30 days under "Restore the Revolution," secret propaganda and exile lectures, and FY-1960/1961 financing (900,000 and 3,500,000) for political, propaganda, paramilitary, and intelligence work. Assesses the regime is consolidating control, economic trouble will cause dislocation not collapse, and Bloc support blocks decisive threats. Cuba poses no direct military threat but may back Latin American subversion. Options weighed: invasion excluded, economic pressure and infiltration judged ineffective or infeasible, deniable paramilitary landing cheapest with guerrilla fallback and doubtful militia reliability. Concludes strong action is needed to prevent Sino-Soviet gains.

Covers the CIA's covert Cuba project: ad hoc training of Cuban personnel in Miami and Washington; weak security and compartmentation; operational failures including the Bay of Pigs (timing, exposed camps, American fliers killed) and Inspector General recommendations; a 1960 plan to replace Castro with a U.S.-acceptable government, with funding and opposition groups; and assessments that invasion is excluded, a deniable paramilitary landing is cheapest, and strong action is needed against Sino-Soviet gains.

Declassified CIA-style material on the 1961 Bay of Pigs and Cuba operations: failed or mismanaged airdrops (most supplies captured, poor coordination, weak Cuban aircrews) and the maritime boat program (Barbara J mutiny, costs, Key West problems). Also covers paramilitary training of Cuban exiles in Guatemala, Panama and New Orleans (poor instruction, morale collapse, delayed infiltration), approval bottlenecks, the 28 March halt of clandestine drops, and 1960 plans to replace Castro with a U.S.-acceptable government.

nodes.title: APPENDIX - A
key_items: A. CLANDESTINE SPTLTRATION BY SEA OF SMALL GROUPS (UP TO 50 MEN)
nodes.summary: Covers clandestine sea infiltration of small guerrilla groups (up to 50 men) into Cuba. Only the Sierra Escambray (Las Villas) and Sierra Maestra (Oriente) have suitable terrain, with Escambray preferred due to air support distance. Government forces are heavy in both provinces, militia has destroyed small insurgent landings, and repeated landings would be detected and likely fail, and vessels risk destruction by Cuban forces.

summary: Covers the Miami Operating Base (WH/4), activated April 1960 as a forward base for Cuban exile liaison and law enforcement coordination, with confused headquarters relations and duplicated efforts. Describes overlapping Headquarters and Miami operations, the CI and PM buildup to 160 staff, Havana Station's closure, and a May 1961 call for single control. Details the WH/4 Branch's Cuba role, Havana's stay-behind agent net, the flawed September 1960 G-2 unit, the poorly supported FRD opposition front, and Bay of Pigs airdrop and boat program failures. Also covers exile training problems, the March 1961 drop halt, 1960 regime-change plans, and the infeasibility of sea infiltration into Escambray and Sierra Maestra.

title: 6. In the Sierra Escambray, which is the only area of
summary: In the Sierra Escambray, the only true guerrilla area in Cuba, ill-equipped untrained bands of 200-300 men struggle to survive and act effectively, serving mainly as a symbol of resistance; smaller groups would also be ineffective. Few south-coast sites allow small-boat landings, mostly at river mouths guarded by machine-gun militia posts, so a small landing group would likely suffer heavy casualties.

title: 8. Small-scale infiltrations would not produce a
summary: Argues that small-scale infiltrations would not trigger general uprisings against Castro, so his regime can only be overthrown short of U.S. military intervention by producing conditions that break the armed forces' obedience. Describes the CIA-trained Cuban Assault Force of volunteers, which is combat-capable as a unit but cannot be committed piecemeal, and notes the U.S. has no legal command over it. Warns that infiltration would cause heavy loss of life through superior enemy forces and summary execution, and would achieve no effective military or psychological result.

title: PROPOSED OPERATION AGAINST CUBA
summary: Describes a 1960s-era proposed operation against Cuba: a preparatory action launched about a year earlier covering organizing broad opposition to the Castro regime, a propaganda campaign, support for peaceful and violent resistance, and building paramilitary ground and air volunteer forces. The text reports that the FRD was formed as a unifying body but drew political refusals, so a broader revolutionary council was pursued, negotiations with Cuban leaders are advancing toward a provisional government with a political platform reflecting the original 26th of July movement goals, a decision on future activities and assets is pending.

title: Military: The
summary: The text describes military paramilitary force readiness. A reinforced unit of 850 personnel will be raised to about 1,000 by adding one more infantry company, used mainly for logistics and as a reserve. Separately, a briefly trained paramilitary force of about 160 is intended for diversionary night landing operations, to be undertaken in advance of the battalion's commitment.

Forces could be combat-ready by 1 April but must withdraw by early April due to volunteer morale, the rainy season, and Guatemalan government limits. summary: Assesses Cuba's military as weak, especially Navy and Air Force, though jet aircraft deliveries and trained pilots are expected within months. Government retains capacity to suppress small guerrilla groups and monitor dissent, so violent opposition will likely be gradually suppressed. Within about six months, overthrowing the Castro regime may become infeasible without a larger organized force than Cuban exiles can recruit. Introduces four alternative courses of action using a paramilitary force, the first minimizing the appearance of outside invasion.

title: TO. PSEC RE
summary: Describes a planned paramilitary operation against Castro's Cuba: options include a surprise landing with tactical air support to spark a revolt or sustain guerrilla war, two successive landings, a whole-force landing to hold a beachhead, covert night infiltration with no heavy weapons, a full-force amphibious assault with a concurrent beachhead and provisional government, a diversionary landing, and a slow build-up in remote terrain needing air cover. Concludes Castro will not fall on his own, and an effective Cuban paramilitary force has a good chance of overthrow without direct U.S. intervention.

It lists the copy distribution (President, Secretary of State, Adolph Berle, Thomas Mann, Secretary of Defense, Lemitzer, McGeorge Bundy, DD/P, Wm. Bundy, Gen. Gray, Mr. Barnes, DD/P subject file on Cuba, D/MCI) with retained or destroyed status, and is marked copy 15 of 17.

title: REVISED CUBAN OPERATION
key_items: a. An MERESGUBSUAAE Landing: The
summary: Revised Cuban operation plan (1961-era, declassified). Political requirements: landing should be unspectacular, at night, without air support, resembling a guerrilla infiltration rather than a WWII-style amphibious assault; need a base for tactical air ops on an airstrip in held territory; slower build-up tempo; terrain suited for guerrilla warfare. Five areas studied; one central mainland beachhead chosen (swamp-protected, near island center, with one or two B-26-capable airstrips, good beaches, history of guerrilla resistance); others rejected for geography, enemy concentrations, or poor estuary. Phases: night landing with no known enemy; dawn movement of tactical aircraft and C-46s with fuel and maintenance; then tanks and supplies once air protection exists, with counterattacks expected in 24-48 hours; breakout later in three possible directions. Provisional government installed in beachhead as soon as aircraft can land.

summary: Excerpt from a 1961-style military planning document on a proposed nighttime paramilitary landing in Cuba's Oriente Province. Covers military advantages (surprise, no known communications, proximity to rear air and sea logistics bases, but gradual force buildup since no local population to recruit from), political acceptability (landing kept low-key, no tactical air support until an airstrip is secured), and the likely need for air command, including opposition acquiring obsolescent combat aircraft and possible pre-landing strafing runs on Castro's air force.

summary: A 1961 declassified-style page (page 8 of 8) concludes that the outlined operation, though revised to meet political requirements, still carries political cost: accusations from Communists and criticism from others are unavoidable when introducing military resources into Cuba to overthrow the regime. The plan aims to minimize political cost without impairing its soundness or chance of success. The alternative is demobilizing the paramilitary force and returning members to the United States, which also carries certain risks.

title: CUBAN OPERATION
summary: Describes a proposed covert operation to overthrow Castro's Cuban government, framed as growing internal resistance aided by defectors, infiltrated weapons and small groups, and external support organized under the Revolutionary Council led by Miro Cardona. To minimize the appearance of invasion, public statements stress that Cubans must overthrow Castro free of U.S. Government control, and air operations are scaled back to limited activity on D-2 and later.

summary: OCR-garbled excerpt of a 1961 CIA document on the Bay of Pigs (Cuba) operation. Covers the D-Day timetable (staging, B-26 defection airstrikes, diversionary landings in Oriente and Pinar del Rio, night landings), cancellation/diversion plans at sea, naval protection, defection outreach to about 31 military/police figures, roughly 7,000 internal insurgents with airdrop and sabotage plans, radio propaganda expansion, the political leadership roster and provisional government plans, CIA command control, and the start of a 20 November 1961 survey memo to McCone.

title: ‘MEMORANDUM FOR:
summary: A 20 November 1961 memo from CIA Inspector General Lyman Kirkpatrick to DCI McCone transmits a 150-page survey of the Cuban operation (Bay of Pigs). It explains the report seeks to find what went wrong and why, without assessing individuals, and includes five annexes and ten corrective recommendations. The review is based on all files, Taylor Committee materials and minutes, and interviews with project officers. The author calls it fair but critical, faults CIA for blaming others, and holds distribution pending McCone's instructions; the PFIAB requested a copy for a December 9 meeting.

title: SUBJECT
summary: Describes the Cuban Operation report prepared under the Inspector General's personal direction, with input from deputy David Mantellas and three officers who collected information and prepared the text. The report draws on agency materials, Taylor Committee documents and minutes, and WH Division records. It confines inspection to internal agency matters, except outside actions affecting the operation. Interviews began with Mr. Esterline and Colonel Hawkins within a week of the operation, with the aim of covering all persons connected to it.

summary: A 28 November 1961 memo from Inspector General Lyman B. Kirkpatrick, cc'd to the DDCI. It says the operation involved the appropriate supervisors, including the A/DDP/A, DD/P, the DD/P Chief, and the WH Chief, plus about 130 other officers and employees. Extensive notes and material from these discussions are documented in the files.

title: MEMORANDUM FOR THE RECORD
summary: A 27 November memorandum for the record: General Cabell directed that the IG report on Cuba be restricted to a need-to-know basis, with no copies beyond those already distributed to McCone, Dulles, Cabell, Bissell, Colonel King and Esterline, unless authorized by the DCI or DDCI. The restriction also applies to the President's Board of Intelligence Advisors and to Mr. Kirkpatrick. Cabell discussed holding the report tightly with Dulles and Bissell, who will pass guidance to King and Esterline. Signed C. P. Cabell, General, USAF, Deputy Director.

title: 1 December 1961
summary: A 1961 memo from Inspector General Lyman Kirkpatrick to the Director of Central Intelligence on the Cuban operation (Bay of Pigs). It argues CIA should not bear sole blame for failure, citing three factors: the U.S. government's lack of recognition of the operation's required magnitude to overthrow Castro; its failure to plan for all contingencies, including committing regular U.S. military forces if exiles could not succeed; and its unwillingness to commit necessary resources for success.

title: 15 December 1961
key_items: SUBJECT: The Inspector General's Survey of the Cuban Operation
summary: A 1961 memo by Deputy Director C. P. Cabell responding to the Inspector General's survey of the Cuban operation (Bay of Pigs). He says detailed commentary would be lengthy and notes inaccuracies, omissions, and unsupported conclusions. General Taylor's group already covered non-tradecraft issues using full testimony, and the IG report conflicts with it. Dulles and Cabell were not consulted. The IG report tries to do too much by treating policy-making as logic, and too little by ignoring the Agency's wider intelligence and covert programs against Castro. It lacks objectivity and could unfairly attack the Agency. He recommends a new report based on complete testimony, focused on clandestine tradecraft.
